title: Bodhisattva Guanyin in the Form of the Buddha Mother

source.label: Metropolitan Museum record (via Commons): Hanging scroll; ink on paper

work.text: As early as 1616, when he was eighteen sui, he produced a series of twelve illustrations depicting legendary figures in poetry of the [fourth century] B.C. known as the [Elegies] of Ch‘u

source.author: Fang Chao-ying
source.title: Ch‘ên Hung-shou
source.publisher: in Arthur W. Hummel (ed.), Eminent Chinese of the Ch‘ing Period, vol. I, US Government Printing Office (Internet Archive scan)

work.text: at the age of four, seeing in his grandfather's establishment a newly-whitewashed wall, forthwith climbed upon a table and drew a full-length portrait of the great general Kuan Yu (now the God of War) of the Han dynasty, from eight to nine feet in height.

moment.text: Cundī Esotericism was also widely practiced by Chinese Buddhist laypersons during the Ming. … She is also prominent in the art of the late Ming, such as in the paintings of Chen Hongshou (1598–1652).
moment.lead: The “Buddha Mother” of the title is Cundi (Zhunti):

matters.text: In his later life he devoted himself chiefly to drawings of Buddhist divinities, particularly Kuan-yin and Lo-han.

source.author: Fang Chao-ying
source.title: Ch‘ên Hung-shou
source.publisher: in Arthur W. Hummel (ed.), Eminent Chinese of the Ch‘ing Period, vol. I, US Government Printing Office (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: Painted when Chen was about twenty-two, this Guanyin shows that the Buddhist devotion of his last years was there from the start: years later he still used a seal calling himself a disciple of Cundi, the deity drawn here.
